Name: subliminal_canary
Title: Subliminal Canaries: Turning Hidden Trait Transmission into a Provenance Watermark for Synthetic Training Data
Short Hypothesis: Because subliminal learning reliably transmits a teacher's steering direction through semantically-innocuous synthetic data, we can deliberately embed a benign, secret 'canary trait' into a synthetic dataset such that ANY model later fine-tuned on that data (even after filtering, paraphrase, or mixing with clean data) inherits a statistically detectable signature. This converts subliminal learning from a threat into a robust, black-box data-provenance watermark that survives keyword sanitation and does not degrade utility.
Related Work: Cloud et al. (2025/Nature 2026) introduced subliminal learning as an unintended pitfall of distillation and showed data filtering fails. Blank et al. (2026) and Hadley & Gultepe (2026) show it is steering-vector distillation with gradients aligning to the teacher's steering direction; Morgulis & Hewitt (2026) show steering-vector teachers transmit precise multi-word biases and that a new steering vector recovered from the laden data has high cosine to the original. Madl (2026) studies auditability of unintended transfer. Dang et al. (2026) extend to agentic trajectories. All prior work treats subliminal transfer as a hazard to detect or block, or as a phenomenon to mechanistically explain. NONE reframe it as a deliberate, controllable provenance mechanism. Existing LLM/data watermarking (e.g., token-distribution watermarks, canary strings, membership inference) either alters visible text (removable by paraphrase/filtering) or embeds detectable strings (removable by sanitation). Our subliminal canary is orthogonal: the mark lives in non-semantic surface structure and is recovered behaviorally from the trained model, not from the text, making it robust precisely where prior watermarks fail. This is a fundamentally new, dual-use reframing distinct from all cited work and from mechanism/defense/capacity/multi-generation studies.
Abstract: Subliminal learning is the surprising transmission of a teacher model's behavioral trait through semantically-unrelated synthetic data such as number sequences, and prior work has treated it purely as a safety hazard. We ask a simple, elegant question: can this hazard be deliberately harnessed as a robust data-provenance watermark? We propose the Subliminal Canary, a procedure that embeds a secret, benign 'canary trait' (e.g., a preference for an arbitrary rare token, defined by a randomly-chosen steering vector) into a synthetic dataset via a lightly-steered teacher, so that any model later fine-tuned on that data acquires a statistically detectable version of the trait. Verification is fully black-box: the auditor queries the suspect model with trait-eliciting prompts and computes a likelihood-ratio test between the canary trait and unused decoy traits, yielding a calibrated false-positive rate. Because subliminal transfer lives in non-semantic structure, the mark survives keyword sanitation, paraphrase, format changes, and dilution with clean data—the exact operations that defeat text-based watermarks and canary strings. We evaluate on Qwen, Llama, and Gemma, measuring detection AUROC and p-values as a function of canary strength, dataset mixing ratio, and adversarial removal attempts, alongside benign-task retention (GSM8K, HumanEval) to confirm the watermark is utility-preserving and behaviorally invisible. We characterize the trade-off between watermark detectability, stealth, and utility, and demonstrate multi-bit capacity by embedding several orthogonal canary directions to encode identifiers. Results establish a new dual-use tool for tracking synthetic-data provenance in distillation pipelines.
Experiments: 1) Canary construction: for each base model (Qwen2.5-7B, Llama-3-8B, Gemma-2-9B), define a secret canary trait as a steering vector trained to maximize likelihood of a rare/arbitrary target behavior (following Morgulis & Hewitt), plus a bank of 20 unused DECOY steering directions for null calibration. Lightly steer the teacher and generate number-sequence, code, and math-reasoning datasets. 2) Baseline transfer + verification: fine-tune a student (matched base) on canary data; verify by an auditor who queries the student with a fixed prompt set and computes a likelihood-ratio / permutation test comparing the canary trait score against the decoy-trait score distribution, producing a p-value and detection AUROC. Confirm mismatched-base students show null (chance) detection (negative control). 3) Robustness to removal operations: apply (a) aggressive keyword/embedding filtering, (b) LLM paraphrase of the data, (c) numeric-format re-encoding, (d) dilution—mix canary data with clean data at ratios 100%/50%/20%/5%/1%; measure detection power (AUROC, p-value) versus each operation and mixing ratio. 4) Utility/stealth: measure benign-task retention (GSM8K subset, HumanEval subset) and check that the canary trait is not obviously exhibited on normal prompts (stealth score = trait activation on generic prompts), quantifying the detectability/stealth/utility trade-off via Pareto curves. 5) Multi-bit capacity: embed k in {1,2,4,8} approximately-orthogonal canary directions to encode a k-bit dataset identifier; measure per-bit decoding accuracy and false-positive rate as k grows, relating to steering-vector orthogonality. 6) Adversarial forgery/spoofing: test whether an adversary without the secret can (a) forge the canary (should fail—requires the secret direction) or (b) scrub it via retraining/regularization; report residual detection power. 7) Sweeps: canary steering strength, LoRA vs full fine-tuning, Adam vs SGD, and number of fine-tune epochs. Metrics: detection AUROC, calibrated p-value / false-positive rate at fixed threshold, cosine similarity between auditor-recovered direction and secret canary, per-bit decoding accuracy, benign-task retention, and stealth score.
Risk Factors and Limitations: 1) Same-base-model requirement: the watermark only survives if the suspect model shares (or is behaviorally matched to) the base used to generate the data, limiting cross-family provenance tracking; we report this scope explicitly and test behavioral-match cases. 2) Detection may be weak at very low mixing ratios (1-5%), setting a practical floor on how diluted watermarked data can be while remaining traceable—we characterize this floor. 3) Dual-use concern: the same mechanism could be used to covertly implant real traits; we restrict canaries to benign rare-token preferences and discuss misuse mitigations. 4) Adaptive adversaries with knowledge that a subliminal watermark exists might apply immunization/orthogonalization defenses (cf. gradient-orthogonalization) to scrub it; we test robustness against such retraining and expect a detectability drop. 5) Multi-bit capacity is bounded by steering-vector orthogonality and may interfere, capping identifier length. 6) Results may be model-family or scale specific; three base models mitigate but do not guarantee frontier-scale generality.
